The company previously traded as FAVO Capital and took its current name in November 2025. In the interview Steward discusses his background, career and investment approach.

stories.headline: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
stories.claim: A letter from 150 figures urges a UK inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution.
stories.summary: A letter signed by 150 scientists, MPs and activists, including Greta Thunberg, urges the government to hold a national inquiry into how air pollution affects lower-income and minority-ethnic communities. Institute for Fiscal Studies research found lower-income areas in England have persistently higher pollution, and minority-ethnic groups are exposed to levels about 6% higher than white populations. Campaign group Mums for Lungs obtained data showing more than 200,000 children were admitted to hospital with breathing difficulties in 11 English areas in 2025, including over 120,000 babies and toddlers. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said air quality is improving and pointed to new targets to cut harmful particle exposure by nearly a third by 2030.

stories.headline: Electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals
stories.claim: UK steelmakers' electricity price premium over France has risen to almost £30/MWh, its highest in three years, per UK Steel.
stories.summary: A lobby group analysis by UK Steel finds British steelmakers' electricity cost premium over French rivals has risen to almost £30 per megawatt hour, the highest level in three years. The group links the widening gap to a surge in global gas prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, since UK power prices are set by gas even when cheaper renewables generate. The gap with France had narrowed to £18/MWh last year, and the gap with Germany fell slightly to about £12 this year. UK Steel director general Peter Brennan argues that direct subsidies are the only realistic fix and has proposed a price cap estimated to cost about £51m a year. The government says it is cutting bills for manufacturers and electricity-intensive firms, and has announced jobs plans for young people in key growth sectors.
key_points: UK steelmakers' electricity premium over France is almost £30/MWh, the highest in three years, according to UK Steel.

The government says it has cut electricity bills for over 10,000 manufacturers and is cutting costs for energy-intensive firms by about £1bn a year.

stories.market_take: Higher UK power costs weigh on British steel producers, and the gap with European rivals could pressure margins.

stories.headline: Time Lords kill leap seconds, before they become the new Y2K bug
stories.claim: The General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to end the use of leap seconds, replacing them with a looser 'Continuous UTC' scheme.
stories.summary: At its 28th meeting, the General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to stop introducing leap seconds to Coordinated Universal Time. The body cited the risk of disruption to Internet of Things devices and critical infrastructure, especially from a possible negative leap second. It warned that industries would need large investment to prepare, comparable to Y2K preparations. The replacement, called Continuous UTC, will allow UT1 and UTC to diverge by up to 3,600 seconds and comes into force next year. The article also notes that digital certificates and network devices could fail if they cannot handle a leap second.

stories.headline: Anthropic is pitching Congress its own AI safety bill, report says
stories.claim: Anthropic is privately lobbying US lawmakers with a draft federal AI safety bill, according to POLITICO.
stories.summary: POLITICO reported that Anthropic has been privately pitching lawmakers a confidential draft bill to regulate frontier AI safety and security, citing three people familiar with the effort. An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has promoted since June. The draft would allow federal officials to halt a model only where it poses a foreseeable, imminent risk of over $1 billion in damages or of killing or seriously injuring more than 50 people, from a bioweapon, a loss of control, or a cyberattack. It would also create outside evaluators, make Commerce the only agency able to seek a halt, and override some state laws. The move comes amid several competing congressional efforts and a debate about AI companies helping to write their own rules.

stories.claim: Researcher names critical Linux KVM guest-to-host escape flaw PwnEscape, rated 9.3 and assigned CVE-2026-99999.
stories.summary: Security researcher Paulos Yibelo has named a Linux KVM flaw PwnEscape and assigned it CVE-2026-99999, rating it 9.3 out of 10 for severity. The bug can allow a guest virtual machine to escape isolation using malformed IPv4 packets, potentially leading to code execution on the host, crashes or memory disclosure. The problem stems from untrusted checksum metadata altering packet headers after validation. AWS says its EC2 service is not at risk and Google Cloud is probably unaffected, and an upstream Linux kernel fix is spreading to major distributions. The article warns that attackers may now study the flaw, so patching is important for Linux users and cloud operators.

An upstream kernel fix exists and is moving into Debian, RHEL and Ubuntu, with virtualisation products such as Proxmox and Nutanix to follow.

stories.claim: Asian AI hardware stocks slump as US chip selloff and financing-cost worries threaten the AI infrastructure spending cycle.

stories.headline: The reason why your drive shows less storage than you paid for
stories.claim: Storage capacity gaps stem mainly from decimal versus binary units, plus operating system and reserved space.
stories.summary: An Engadget explainer says drives often show less usable space than advertised because storage makers count in decimal units (1GB as 1 billion bytes) while Windows uses binary units (1GB as 1,073,741,824 bytes). A 1TB drive appears as about 931GB in Windows but shows full capacity on a Mac. The article notes that operating systems take up substantial space, with iOS 27 using over 22GB on a 128GB iPhone 16 Pro and Windows 11 using over 81GB on a gaming laptop. It adds that Microsoft and Apple have no plans to change their units, so the inconsistency will persist. Rising storage prices driven by AI datacentre demand make the issue more pressing.
key_points: Storage makers usually use decimal units, where 1GB equals one billion bytes.
Windows reports capacity in binary units, so a 1TB drive shows about 931GB.
Operating systems such as iOS 27 and Windows 11 occupy large amounts of space before users install anything.
Microsoft and Apple are not expected to change their unit conventions.
Storage prices are rising, partly because of demand from AI datacentres.

stories.headline: ‘We are suffocating’: protests spread to Lisbon and Milan as housing and living cost tensions intensify
stories.claim: Housing and living-cost protests spread from Spain and France to Milan, Lisbon and Albania, with violence and arrests reported.
stories.summary: Protests over housing costs and living expenses have spread from Spain and France to Italy, Portugal and Albania. In Milan, a Saturday march turned violent, with about 50 people detained and at least two police officers injured. In Lisbon, protesters set up a tent camp in Rossio Square demanding action on housing. Italy's prime minister Giorgia Meloni blamed 'hooligans' for the violence, while Portugal's government said it understood public anger. Albania has seen violent demonstrations over university fees and calls for the prime minister's resignation.
key_points: A Saturday march in Milan over living costs turned violent, with masked rioters throwing stones and setting fire to barricades.
Police used water cannon and teargas in Milan; about 50 demonstrators, many of them minors, were detained and two officers injured.
In Lisbon, hundreds stayed overnight at a tent camp in Rossio Square, following a nationwide march of thousands.
Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, roughly twice the EU average, according to official data.
In Albania, protests over university conditions and tuition fees turned violent, with police using rubber bullets for the first time.
In Spain, a snap general election has been called for late November after housing measures were voted down in parliament.
stories.story:
Protests over the cost of living and housing have spread beyond Spain and France into Italy, Portugal and Albania, in some cases turning violent. In Milan, a march against rising living costs that began peacefully ended with masked people throwing stones and paving blocks at riot police and setting fire to barricades made of bar tables. Police responded with water cannon and teargas, and at least two officers were hurt. The LaPresse news agency reported about 50 detentions, many of those held being minors. Prime minister Giorgia Meloni said the right to protest did not extend to setting cities alight and accused hooligans of exploiting the demonstrations. Milan's centre-left mayor, Giuseppe Sala, said the grievances were understandable but the violence was not justifiable.

In Lisbon, a tent camp similar to one set up in Madrid weeks earlier appeared in Rossio Square after a nationwide march drew thousands. Protesters said they were struggling with rents and housing costs. Official data shows Portuguese housing prices rose 124% between 2015 and 2024, about twice the EU average. Portugal's prime minister, Luís Montenegro, said his government understood public frustration but warned rivals against importing unrest seen in France. A protest camp in Porto had already been set up earlier.

In Albania, demonstrators angry over university conditions and high tuition fees have demanded the resignation of prime minister Edi Rama. Protesters threw rocks and petrol bombs, torched cars and set buildings on fire, including a court, banks and a post office. Police used rubber bullets for the first time in the protests, which follow months of anti-government demonstrations.

The unrest traces back to Spain, where an 87-year-old woman was evicted after failing to pay a 230% rent increase, sparking protests and a camp in Madrid. The government's emergency housing measures were voted down in congress, and prime minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for late November. In France, a movement that began over school conditions has grown into a nationwide protest against inequality, with more than 1,200 people arrested on Saturday. Whether these protests widen further or fade will depend largely on how governments respond to housing and living cost pressures.
stories.market_take: Broader political unrest in Europe could weigh modestly on sentiment towards euro-area bonds and property-linked shares.

stories.claim: Andrew Left seeks to overturn his fraud conviction after a prosecution witness, Bachus, became linked to an insider trading probe.
stories.summary: Short-seller Andrew Left is asking for his securities fraud conviction to be overturned after a key witness, Bachus, reportedly became caught up in an insider trading investigation. stories.story:
Andrew Left, a short seller whose securities fraud conviction was secured after a trial in Los Angeles, is seeking to have that verdict overturned. His lawyers argue that a witness, identified as Bachus, became caught up in an insider trading investigation, which they say calls the conviction into question.

According to court filings, the prosecution told Left's lawyers that it did not learn about the investigation until after the trial had finished. It is not clear which government agency opened the probe, or when Bachus or Grand Canyon Education became aware of it. Many of the relevant documents remain sealed or redacted on the court docket.

Justice Department prosecutors have pushed back. They say Left's lawyers overstated Bachus's part in the case, which involved alleged securities fraud linked to more than a dozen public companies. Prosecutors argued that Left wanted to carry out his own 'shadow investigation' into Bachus to discredit him, and said the law does not allow fishing expeditions in search of a claim.

Left declined to comment. His attorney, Eric S. Rosen, said he could not comment because key documents remain under seal. A spokesperson for the US Attorney's office in Los Angeles also declined to comment. The next steps will depend on how the court handles the sealed material and whether it accepts the argument that the undisclosed probe affects the verdict.
stories.market_take: Limited direct market effect, though the case touches on short-selling and securities fraud enforcement.

stories.story:
The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor the first British data centre of Nscale, the AI cloud startup, in Loughton, Essex. The move comes as Nscale prepares to go public, and Bloomberg, citing the Telegraph, says the site has faced a series of delays. The Telegraph did not give a reason for Microsoft's decision. Microsoft did not comment to the Telegraph and did not immediately respond to Bloomberg.

The Loughton site has been affected by grid problems. Authorities have reportedly told Nscale not to expect a power supply until the 2030s. The Next Web had reported in July that the grid could not connect the site in time for its planned opening. Nscale says it remains committed to the site, is looking at other power sources and UK locations, and that its relationship with Microsoft is strong and long-term. It says the grid issue does not affect its other contracts.

The IPO is significant. Nscale is seeking to raise as much as $3bn, possibly as soon as this month. Its filing shows Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts. Anthropic agreed in August to spend $45bn on Nscale compute over six years, and Microsoft has signed a letter of intent for a campus in West Virginia. Bloomberg also reports that Nscale's flagship Norway site is six months behind schedule, with only 6.4 megawatts of a planned 30-megawatt facility running.

The wider context is investor caution about neocloud companies, which are racing to build AI computing capacity and often borrow heavily. CoreWeave shares fell 25% last week, their worst week since November, and Australia's Firmus scrapped its IPO after failing to win enough support. Whether Microsoft's withdrawal is confirmed, and how Nscale's listing is priced, will be closely watched.

The piece addresses a common privacy concern about devices that sit in homes and respond to voice.

According to Amazon, Alexa does not transcribe every word. Instead, it listens for acoustic patterns that match its wake word. Only after recognising that wake word does the device begin active listening, record audio and send it to the cloud. The article compares this to hearing one's name in a conversation without catching every other word.

The explainer then sets out options for users. The simplest is to press the microphone-off button on Echo devices, which shows a red light. Users who prefer voice activation can change their recording settings in the Alexa app to keep recordings for three months or 18 months, keep them until deleted, or not retain them at all. Some devices allow deletion by voice, although this does not work on Alexa+ or Amazon Kids devices.

The article stresses that these settings apply only to Amazon's cloud. Third-party devices, such as some robotic vacuums or smart TVs, may still hold data. Deleting voice recordings can also reduce how well Alexa personalises responses, because it cannot keep a voice profile. The piece is consumer guidance rather than a new development, and it has no clear market implications.

stories.headline: Researchers train AI to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals
stories.claim: Swedish Defence Research Agency researchers built WiFireNet, an experimental AI that spots concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal distortion.
stories.summary: Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have developed WiFireNet, an experimental AI system that attempts to detect concealed handguns using Wi-Fi signals rather than cameras or metal detectors. The method analyses channel state information, the way an object alters ambient Wi-Fi as it passes through or reflects signals. In controlled indoor trials the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%, falling to 53.8% under stricter location requirements. The team has released its code, models and dataset as open source, while privacy critics warn about the lack of regulation for Wi-Fi sensing.
key_points: FOI researchers posted a paper on arXiv describing WiFireNet, a system that detects concealed handguns from Wi-Fi signal data.
The system uses a transmitter, a receiver and a deep learning model that reads channel state information.
Average handgun-detection precision was 72.5% in trials with up to four moving people, but fell to 53.8% when exact weapon location was required.

stories.story:
Researchers at the Swedish Defence Research Agency (FOI) have described an experimental artificial intelligence system that aims to identify concealed handguns by analysing how people and objects disturb ordinary Wi-Fi signals. The work was detailed in a paper posted on arXiv on 13 October. The system, named WiFireNet, is positioned as a non-intrusive alternative to visible cameras and metal detectors, which the researchers describe as either conspicuous or cumbersome.

The approach relies on channel state information, the data describing how an object changes Wi-Fi signals through reflection and penetration depending on its shape, orientation and material. To train the model, the team built a dataset called the WiFire Dataset by recording video of people walking with objects, from phones to handguns, while simultaneously capturing Wi-Fi signals. They included a plastic handgun, a metal water bottle, a real metal handgun and a phone so the system could tell a gun apart from similar everyday items.

In controlled trials with up to four moving people in a small indoor space, the system reached an average handgun-detection precision of 72.5%. When the task required pinpointing the weapon's exact position on a person, precision dropped to 53.8%. The neural network also struggled in unfamiliar indoor layouts that it had not been tested on. The researchers stress that the system is still experimental and the prototype used an old wireless standard to prove the concept.

The team has made the code, models and dataset open source to encourage further work, and plans to move to modern Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 8 networks with richer data. The article notes that Wi-Fi sensing is becoming more popular as a surveillance technique because it needs little specialised equipment. Critics argue that its spread, together with the absence of regulatory frameworks, raises serious privacy concerns. The results suggest the technology is far from ready for real-world security use, though it marks a notable research step.

stories.headline: DJI’s first battery-swapping dock gets drones recharged and back in the air in under 45 seconds
stories.claim: DJI has launched the Dock 4 battery-swapping drone dock, paired with the Matrice 5TD, which is not sold in the US.
stories.summary: DJI has unveiled the Dock 4, a drone dock that swaps batteries automatically in about 25 seconds, allowing a drone to be back in the air within 45 seconds of landing. It is aimed at emergency response, which DJI calls dock-as-a-first-responder. The dock works only with the new Matrice 5TD drone and is not FCC-authorised or sold in the US. Chinese partners are taking orders for a kit priced at 167,999 yuan, about $25,000 for the hardware alone. The launch comes amid a US regulatory crackdown on foreign-made drones.
key_points: The Dock 4 swaps drone batteries in about 25 seconds, with a turnaround of under 45 seconds from landing to takeoff.
Each battery pack is rated at 260 Wh and can be charged from 15% to 95% in roughly 27 minutes.
The dock works only with the Matrice 5TD drone and the DJI O4 Ground Station.
The Matrice 5TD carries high-resolution cameras, thermal sensors, LiDAR and a laser rangefinder.
The kit is priced at 167,999 yuan, about $25,000, and is available through Chinese partners.
The FCC added foreign-made drones to its Covered List, so the product cannot be sold in the US.
stories.story:
DJI, the Chinese drone maker, has launched the Dock 4, a battery-swapping drone dock that it says is its first product of this kind. According to a company press release, the dock replaces a drone's battery automatically in about 25 seconds, so the aircraft can take off again within 45 seconds of landing. Without battery swapping, a normal recharge would take around 30 minutes. DJI markets the product for emergency response, calling it a dock-as-a-first-responder solution.

The dock can charge two battery packs at once, each rated at 260 Wh, and estimates say each can be charged from 15% to 95% in about 27 minutes. The packs can also provide backup power for the dock, and with at least two packs loaded the dock can keep swapping batteries during a grid power cut. The dock weighs 66 kg without accessories. It works only with the new Matrice 5TD drone, which carries three 50 MP cameras, thermal sensors, LiDAR, radar and a laser rangefinder, and it can detect 17 types of object.

The kit is available to order from DJI partners in China at 167,999 yuan, roughly $25,000 for the hardware alone. However, the product is not FCC-authorised and cannot be sold in the United States. In December last year the FCC added all foreign-made drones and their critical components to its Covered List, which blocks new models from authorisation unless a US agency certifies they pose no security risk. DJI has sued the commission this year. A separate FCC proposal from August could also remove previously authorised foreign drones with LiDAR or thermal sensors from sale, though no final order had been issued as of 17 October.

The launch underlines how DJI is pushing into automated drone operations for public safety while its US access is restricted. Whether the dock gains a meaningful foothold will depend on how the regulatory dispute develops and on demand from customers outside the US.
stories.market_take: Limited direct effect on listed companies, though US restrictions on DJI's products remain a background risk for drone supply chains.

stories.headline: Flock camera locations revealed on MapQuest’s new Surveillance Layer
stories.claim: MapQuest added a Surveillance Layer to its app showing locations of known licence plate readers from many vendors, including Flock.
stories.summary: MapQuest has released an app update with a new Surveillance Layer that plots known automatic licence plate reader cameras on its map. The layer covers devices from Flock Safety and several other manufacturers, including Motorola Solutions, Genetec, Axis and Axon. It also shows the direction each camera faces, so users can plan routes to avoid them. The company did not explain how it obtained the data. The move reignites debate over privacy and police use of such cameras.
key_points: MapQuest's update adds a Surveillance Layer that marks known licence plate readers on its map.
Covered vendors include Flock, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Rekor and others.
The feature shows each camera's facing direction, which lets users avoid known cameras.
The source of the camera data is unclear, though it resembles a map built by a researcher from Flock's own data.
Critics cite police misuse and administrative errors, and some cities have removed the cameras after complaints.
Police have previously objected to similar features, such as Waze's 2015 police-reporting update.
stories.story:
MapQuest, the long-running online mapping and navigation service, has released an app update that adds a feature called the Surveillance Layer. The company announced the change on Bluesky. When the layer is switched on in the map options, it shows the locations of known automatic licence plate readers, which are cameras that read vehicle registration plates. The list includes devices from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Rekor and several other companies, as well as other outdoor surveillance cameras.

Beyond marking each location, the layer also shows the direction in which each camera faces. This allows drivers who do not want to be recorded to plan routes that avoid known cameras where possible. The article notes, however, that drivers heading to places with dense camera coverage may still pass one. It is not clear how MapQuest gathered the data. A security researcher previously built a Flock surveillance map using Flock's own data, and the article suggests the new feature is similar in nature.

Licence plate readers are widely used by police and cities, which say they help track suspected criminals and improve public safety. Critics, however, describe them as a serious privacy intrusion, pointing to cases where officers misused the systems and to administrative errors, including one that led to an innocent car reviewer being detained. Some cities have reacted to resident complaints by removing the cameras. The article also mentions a Canadian YouTuber who built a camera that tracked police vehicles, and whose efforts drew a visit from officers who raised privacy concerns.

Police departments previously objected when Waze added a feature in 2015 that let users report officers' locations, so there may be pushback against MapQuest's move as well. The article does not say whether any authority has responded. The feature is a clear example of how mapping apps are becoming a route for public scrutiny of surveillance infrastructure, and it is likely to fuel the ongoing privacy debate over licence plate readers.

The story frames negotiation by machines as a new challenge for technology companies.
Tech firms are being forced to confront the rules of negotiation when AI acts for humans.
The available text is only a feed summary, so specifics are limited.

The broader context is the rapid growth of so-called AI agents, which are designed to carry out tasks such as booking, buying or contracting with minimal human input. As these systems take on commercial roles, questions arise about who is bound by an agreement, how consent is recorded and who is liable if an agent makes a mistake.

stories.headline: Typo-squatting attacks with major domains are still viable
stories.claim: Researchers show that a Cyrillic-based lookalike of apple.com can evade Chromium's typosquatting protections.
stories.summary: A Tom's Hardware article, based on research from Have I Been Squatted, shows that the domain 'аррӏө.com' can pass Chromium's anti-spoofing checks despite imitating apple.com. The trick relies on a Cyrillic character, ө, which is not on Chromium's list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters. The article explains how Chromium's rules work and where they fall short. It concludes that companies should register lookalike domains and encourage passkeys, which are bound to specific domains.
key_points: The domain аррӏө.com evades Chromium's protections because the character ө is not on its list of 29 confusable Cyrillic characters.
Chromium shows Punycode for mixed-alphabet lookalikes and blocks all-Cyrillic lookalikes from the list.
A 2020 study found Chromium caught 64.1% of lookalike attempts, ahead of Firefox and Safari.
Chromium checks over 8,000 popular domains, with stronger checks on 836 of them.
Researchers recommend registering lookalike domains and using passkeys, which only work on their registered domain.
stories.story:
Tom's Hardware reports on research by Have I Been Squatted, which shows that typosquatting attacks using internationalised domain names remain viable. The researchers used the domain аррӏө.com, which looks like apple.com but is not identical to it, to show that a specific combination of Cyrillic characters can slip past several layers of protection in Chromium-based browsers.

The weakness is subtle. Chromium blocks domains that mix alphabets, displaying them in Punycode instead, and it also keeps a list of 29 Cyrillic characters that closely resemble Latin letters. Using only those characters is blocked. The character ө, however, is not on that list, which lets the test domain pass. The article notes that a future Chromium release could close the gap.

The piece places the issue in the wider history of internationalised domain names, which the IETF allowed in order to support non-Latin scripts. Those same scripts contain many visually similar characters, which makes detection hard. A 2020 study cited in the article found Chromium caught 64.1% of lookalike attempts, with Firefox and Safari behind it. Chromium underpins Chrome, Edge and Brave.

The researchers advise companies worried about impersonation to register lookalike domains and to encourage passkey use, since passkeys are tied to a specific domain and will not work on a fake site. The article suggests that no rule set can fully solve the problem, so defence will remain a matter of layered measures.

stories.headline: Why you might not want to join two Ethernet cables (and what you should do instead)
stories.claim: Joining Ethernet cables with couplers can cause problems, so a single longer cable or a switch is usually better.
stories.summary: Engadget advises against joining two Ethernet cables with a coupler for permanent setups, since the extra connection can cause dropouts or drop speeds. A single longer cable is simpler, and a network switch is better when more wired ports are needed. The article cites trueCABLE tests showing that four couplers failed while three generally passed. It also notes the 100-metre copper length limit, which a coupler cannot extend.
key_points: A coupler is simply two RJ45 sockets joined together and does not boost signal.
Each extra join is a potential failure point, causing dropouts or falling back to 100 Mbps.
The standard copper Ethernet channel limit is 100 metres (328 feet), including patch cords.
trueCABLE tests found configurations with four couplers failed, while three generally passed.
An unmanaged five-port Gigabit switch can cost around $15 and needs no configuration.
stories.story:
Engadget offers practical advice for anyone whose Ethernet cable has become too short after moving a desk or equipment. A small RJ45 coupler can join two cables together without needing power or configuration, and a good-quality coupler should not noticeably slow a connection. However, the article argues that the coupler adds a connection that can fail, particularly if it is cheap or easily knocked.

Symptoms of a poor join can include occasional dropouts, transmission errors, or a link that falls back from 1 Gbps to 100 Mbps. The advice is to test with a good cable without the coupler before troubleshooting the router or contacting an internet provider. A coupler also does not extend the length limit, which is 100 metres for copper Ethernet including patch cords.

The article cites testing by trueCABLE using a Fluke DSX-8000 tester on Cat6 and Cat6A cables. Configurations with three couplers generally passed, one only marginally, while those with four failed. The results depend on the specific parts used, but they suggest that adding joins unnecessarily is a poor idea.

For a permanent setup, the recommendation is a single cable of the right length, routed with some slack. Where a cable already runs to a room with several devices, a small unmanaged switch is the better choice, since each port creates a separate link with its own distance limit. Anyone installing a camera or wireless access point should also check for Power over Ethernet support, as a standard switch will not supply power.

stories.headline: Supreme Court appears open to wider video privacy law in Paramount case
stories.claim: US Supreme Court justices appeared inclined to back a viewer's wider reading of the Video Privacy Protection Act against Paramount.
stories.summary: During oral argument in Salazar v. Paramount Global, the US Supreme Court justices appeared open to a broad reading of the Video Privacy Protection Act. The plaintiff says a Paramount website sent his video viewing history to Facebook via Meta's Pixel without consent, and seeks a class action with damages of up to $2,500 per person. Paramount's lawyer argued the law was designed for video rentals, not web advertising. A ruling is expected by next summer.
key_points: The justices heard arguments in Salazar v. Paramount Global and appeared receptive to the plaintiff.
The plaintiff says Meta's Pixel sent his video history to Facebook without consent.
He seeks a class action with damages of up to $2,500 per person.
The Video Privacy Protection Act dates from 1988 and followed the Robert Bork rental-records episode.
Paramount argued that applying the law to web tracking would create a broad internet privacy regime.
A ruling is expected by next summer.
stories.story:
The US Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday in Salazar v. Paramount Global, a case that could widen privacy liability for websites that use tracking tools on video pages. According to reports cited in the article, the justices appeared inclined to side with the plaintiff, while Paramount's case did not seem to persuade them.

The plaintiff alleges that a Meta tracking tool known as the Pixel on a Paramount website sent details of the videos he watched to Facebook without his consent. He wants to bring a class action seeking up to $2,500 per person under the Video Privacy Protection Act, a 1988 law passed after a journalist published the video rental history of Supreme Court nominee Robert Bork.

Paramount's lawyer, Paul Clement, argued that the plaintiff's reading would turn a law about video rentals into a sweeping internet privacy regime, and warned that sites might have to put videos behind consent walls. Justice Kagan suggested websites had two simple options, obtaining consent or stopping the sale of private data. Justice Sotomayor said gating videos would leave the choice to users. Justice Kavanaugh questioned whether it was right to repurpose a video law for web advertising tracking, and said consent would be over-broad.

If the plaintiff wins, the article says more lawsuits could follow against sites using tracking tools on video pages. The article also notes that Paramount, which recently won approval for its Warner Bros deal, is not the only media company facing viewer lawsuits, with Twitch and Amazon facing a separate class action over AI training on livestreams. A decision is expected by next summer.
stories.market_take: Paramount faces potential privacy liability that could weigh modestly on the stock if a ruling goes against it.

stories.headline: 300-plus local data center bans have only delayed just three US projects
stories.claim: A SemiAnalysis report says over 300 local data centre moratoriums have delayed only a small share of planned US capacity.
stories.summary: SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data centre moratoriums have had little effect on US buildout, with only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas likely to be delayed. Its 2027 forecast of 38 GW has barely moved in 12 months. The firm says moratoriums would need to be far more widespread and restrictive to slow the buildout. It also flags a Texas state-level pause on permits as a factor it has not fully counted.
key_points: Only about 2.3 GW of 21 GW in moratorium areas is likely to be delayed, according to SemiAnalysis.
The 2027 US data centre IT capacity forecast stands at 38 GW, more than double 2026.
Over 400 local moratorium measures are tracked across 17 states as of September.
Moratoriums often miss the site, permit or timeline, and do not revoke existing approvals.
A Texas Commission on Environmental Quality pause on data centre permits is not included in the 2.3 GW figure.
Public opinion in an August poll was more negative than positive about data centres.
stories.story:
A report from SemiAnalysis, shared on X and summarised by Tom's Hardware, argues that more than 300 local data centre construction moratoriums have done little to slow the US buildout. Of about 21 GW of data centre capacity located in moratorium areas, the firm estimates only around 2.3 GW is likely to be delayed. Its forecast of 38 GW of US data centre IT capacity for 2027, more than double 2026, has barely moved over the past year.

The firm defines a moratorium as a temporary legal pause, usually a freeze on accepting new applications. It tracks more than 400 local measures across 17 states, including some permanent zoning bans. New York, Texas, Pennsylvania and Oregon all acted within under two months this summer. The analysis found that moratoriums often do not reach the parcel, overlap the timeline or cover a project's use, and they do not revoke existing approvals. Michigan, for example, has 45 enacted moratoriums but effectively no pipeline exposure.

The report also highlights a Texas state pause. Governor Greg Abbott told the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to issue no permits for data centre projects, and law firm Bracewell expects it to last until the grid operator ERCOT completes its review in mid-December. The 2.3 GW figure excludes this pause, so the analysis may understate the effect. The article says the firm would be more worried by a strict state-level moratorium that also blocked off-grid projects.

SemiAnalysis concludes that moratoriums could delay the buildout but are not yet at scale. An Economist reporter quoted in the piece described them as much more bark than bite for now, with the bigger risk being a deterrent to newer projects. Public sentiment is also a factor, with an August poll by the firm showing more negative than positive views of data centres. The next checkpoint is a TCEQ compliance report to the governor's office.
stories.market_take: The analysis suggests the US data centre buildout is largely intact, though the Texas permit pause is a watch point for energy and infrastructure names.

stories.headline: Anthropic’s proposed AI safety bill only kicks in if 50 deaths or $1 billion in damages are on the line
stories.claim: Anthropic is lobbying for an AI safety bill that would let the government block model releases only for risks of over $1bn damage or over 50 casualties.
stories.summary: Politico reports that Anthropic is lobbying for a federal AI safety bill that would allow the government to block a model's release only when it poses a risk of $1 billion in damages or killing or injuring over 50 people. An independent third-party evaluator registered with the Commerce Department would assess the lab. Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework. The article places the proposal against recent AI safety concerns and congressional proposals.
key_points: The bill would allow blocking a model release only if risk exceeds $1 billion in damages or harm to over 50 people.
Covered risks include bioweapons, AI-enabled cyberattacks and loss of control over AI models or agents.
An independent evaluator registered with the Commerce Department would review the lab periodically.
Evaluators must report potential risks within 72 hours, and a federal court in DC would decide on any halt.
Anthropic says the bill reflects its Advanced AI Framework, advocated since June.
The bill is a proposal and has not been passed by Congress.
stories.story:
Politico, as cited by Tom's Hardware, reports that Anthropic is lobbying for an AI safety bill that would give the US government power to block an AI model's release only in narrow circumstances. The threshold is a risk of at least $1 billion in damages, or the killing or injuring of more than 50 people. An independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would evaluate the lab and its models periodically, and the lab could pay for those evaluations as long as this did not compromise the evaluator's independence.

The proposal names three categories of risk: the creation or release of a bioweapon, AI-enabled or AI-assisted cyberattacks, and an AI lab losing control of a model or agents. If an evaluator sees a possible such event, it must report to the Commerce Department within 72 hours. The department would then present the evidence to a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would decide whether the release should be halted. The bill would also bar other departments, agencies or officers from ordering an AI lab to stop releasing a model.

An Anthropic spokesperson said the bill reflects the company's Advanced AI Framework, which it has pushed with federal and state lawmakers since June, and described the policies as sensible. The article places the proposal in a climate of growing concern about AI safety, citing reported incidents involving OpenAI models, comments from Anthropic's chief executive about botnet risks, and a congressional proposal to require kill switches on the most powerful models.

The piece also mentions a separate proposal from Senator Bernie Sanders that would impose a 20-year prison term for developing AI superintelligence. The Anthropic bill would be one more measure for Congress to consider, and it is not yet law. The article does not give a timetable for a vote.
stories.market_take: Any federal AI safety rules could affect AI developers, though the proposal is at an early stage.

stories.summary: Google DeepMind reported that four AI agents running on Gemini 4 Argon beat Minecraft, including defeating the Ender Dragon, without human help or assigned roles. The agents organised their own tasks, warned each other of threats, recovered items from fallen teammates and logged mistakes in shared memory. The run lasted 27 hours and 14 minutes, during which the agents wrote 2,783 JavaScript programs, exchanged 229 chat messages and died 605 times. The session would cost $1,620 at a standard Gemini 4 Argon price due to take effect in 2027. No roles, strategies or game-specific tools were given to the agents.
The agents coordinated by splitting tasks, warning of threats and recovering items from dead teammates.
The run took 27 hours 14 minutes, with 2,783 JavaScript programs written and 605 deaths.
The cost would be $1,620 at a standard price set to take effect in 2027.
The outlet frames it as part of a trend of general agentic models beating games once needing purpose-built systems.
stories.story:
Google's DeepMind team has reported that four AI agents running on the Gemini 4 Argon model completed Minecraft for the first time without any human input. The agents were placed in a randomly generated world with no assigned roles, strategies or game-specific tools. Over the course of the run they divided the work among themselves, warned one another about threats, retrieved items from teammates who had died and recorded their errors in a shared memory store. The session ended with the Ender Dragon defeated, which is the game's final boss.

The run was long and messy. It lasted 27 hours and 14 minutes and involved 2,783 JavaScript programs written by the agents, 229 chat messages between them and 605 deaths in total. The article estimates the session would have cost $1,620 at the standard Gemini 4 Argon price, which is due to take effect in 2027 rather than now.

The achievement is part of a wider pattern. The article notes that only a few years ago, video game performance of this kind typically required specialised AI systems trained from scratch for a single game. Now general-purpose agentic models are increasingly managing similar tasks. The report is a demonstration rather than a commercial product launch, and it does not say whether the approach will be released to the public. Readers should treat the cost figure as an estimate based on a future price.

stories.headline: Skip Intel Googlebooks for now, because your favorite apps and games may run poorly on them
stories.claim: Google says 96.6% of the top Android apps run on Intel Googlebooks, while Intel and Google dispute the cause of compatibility gaps.
stories.summary: Google and Intel are publicly disagreeing over app performance on Intel-based Googlebooks, a line of Android laptops. Google says a small number of complex apps, mainly games using Arm-only native code, need developer tuning, and that 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without issues on Intel Googlebooks. Intel responded by pointing to its Intel Bridge Technology translation layer and said it expects strong compatibility and fast performance. The article explains that Arm-based Snapdragon Googlebooks avoid translation, while Intel models must translate Arm instructions in real time, which can reduce frame rates in demanding native apps. The article advises buyers to check processor type before purchase.
key_points: Google says 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used Android apps run without issues on Intel Googlebooks.
Just over 300 popular apps are unavailable, mostly because they do not suit large screens, Google says.
Intel says its Intel Bridge Technology translation layer is built on ChromeOS technology without a virtual machine.
Dell and HP use Qualcomm Arm chips, while Acer, ASUS and Lenovo use Intel Panther Lake x86 chips.
Native Arm code in some games must be translated on Intel chips, which can cut frame rates.
Demanding games and emulators are likely to be the weakest spots on Intel models.
stories.story:
Google and Intel have publicly traded views on whether Android apps run well on Googlebooks, the Android-based laptops launched in October 2026. Google told Android Authority that most Android apps run smoothly on both Intel and Qualcomm models, but that a small number of complex apps or games need developer tuning on Intel hardware. It said it is working with developers, Intel and Qualcomm to improve compatibility. In a later statement it put a figure on the issue, saying 96.6% of its 10,000-plus most-used apps run without problems on Intel Googlebooks.

Intel responded to Gizmodo by stressing its Intel Bridge Technology. It said the translation layer uses the same underlying technology as ChromeOS but without a virtualised runtime, and that it expects users to see strong app compatibility and fast performance. The chipmaker credited its work on the Android framework and its Linux and open-source expertise. The article notes that about 300 popular apps are unavailable on Intel models, though Google says most of these are missing because they do not work on large screens rather than because of the chip.

The disagreement comes down to chip architecture. Android was built around Arm processors, and many apps, particularly games, contain native code compiled only for Arm. Dell and HP Googlebooks use Qualcomm's Arm-based Snapdragon X Elite, which runs this code directly. Acer, ASUS and Lenovo models use Intel's x86-based Panther Lake chips, which must translate Arm instructions in real time. On older Intel Chromebooks this approach felt sluggish, and the new Googlebook system removes the virtual machine but keeps the translation step. Apps written in Java or Kotlin generally run without trouble, so the issue mainly affects performance-heavy native code.

For buyers, the practical advice is to check the processor before purchase. Everyday tasks and streaming should be fine on Intel models, while demanding games such as Genshin Impact and emulators may struggle. Both companies are expected to release updates to narrow the gaps, though the timing is not stated.
stories.market_take: The dispute could slightly weigh on Intel's Googlebook appeal against Qualcomm-based models.

stocks.reason: Its Arm-based Snapdragon chips in Dell and HP Googlebooks avoid translation overhead.

stories.headline: World Bank backs ‘small AI’ on phones for poorer nations, Guardian reports
stories.claim: The World Bank is encouraging developing countries to adopt compact 'small AI' models that run on basic phones.
stories.summary: The World Bank's chief knowledge officer, Paschal Donohoe, has urged developing countries to build 'small AI', which are compact, task-specific models that run on phones with weak signals. He said such tools could speed up growth in emerging economies if they fit local needs and languages. He gave the example of Indian farmers needing soil analysis in their own language. The IMF's Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first provide power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. The article also notes large infrastructure gaps and warns that AI could change or remove 40% of jobs worldwide over time.
key_points: Donohoe says compact 'small AI' models should run on phones with weak signals and in local languages.
He argues AI could bring growth within decades that might otherwise take centuries.
Indian farmers in the World Bank's AgriConnect scheme are cited as a use case for soil analysis.
IMF chief Georgieva says power, digital infrastructure and protection from misuse must come first.
Georgieva warned 40% of jobs could be changed or removed by AI over time, with entry-level roles most at risk.
The World Bank says it raised $120bn in private capital over the past year as some rich countries cut aid.
stories.story:
The World Bank wants developing countries to focus on what it calls 'small AI': compact models trained on narrow data for a single task, which can run on a mobile phone even when the signal is weak. Paschal Donohoe, the bank's chief knowledge officer and a former Irish finance minister, said the technology could speed up growth in emerging economies, provided it suits local needs. He suggested that development that might once have taken centuries could happen within decades.

Donohoe gave the example of farmers in India within the bank's AgriConnect scheme, who need soil analysis in their own language. He argued there will never be enough agricultural experts to serve every small farm, and said such products could come from the World Bank, governments and private firms working together. The remarks followed discussions on AI at the World Bank and IMF meetings in Bangkok earlier this month.

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said governments must first put in place power, digital infrastructure and protection from bad actors. She argued that if these basics are in place, AI adoption could be as democratic as the mobile phone. The gaps are large, however. A World Bank report from August found almost a third of rural schools in sub-Saharan Africa had no electricity. Georgieva also warned that around 40% of jobs worldwide could be changed or eliminated by AI over time, with young people starting out facing the greatest risk as entry-level roles shrink.

Donohoe said the bank had raised $120bn in private capital over the past year at a time when countries including the US and UK have reduced aid budgets. The article is based on a Guardian report and the remarks are policy aspirations rather than announced programmes with set funding.

stories.story:
A report says Nvidia is developing a custom form of high-bandwidth memory, called NVHBM, and has asked the major memory makers to change how they build it. Under the proposal, Samsung, Micron and SK hynix would make the base die of the memory stack on TSMC's 3nm process, rather than each using their own process. The core die would use the sixth-generation 1c DRAM process. The idea is that one common base die would make performance more consistent and mean Nvidia does not need to separately verify each supplier's samples, saving time.

According to the report, Samsung has agreed, which would be a notable change for a company that has traditionally developed its HBM core and base dies in-house. Samsung is reportedly still keeping its own foundry as an option in case demand for NVHBM exceeds TSMC's production capacity. Standard HBM development would continue within Samsung. The article also says Nvidia has claimed the custom design could deliver up to 30% more memory bandwidth than standard HBM4E while drawing up to 15% less power. These are described as the company's own promises and the article does not give independent testing.

The article links the story to Nvidia's upcoming Feynman GPUs, which are said to use the custom HBM. It also notes that memory has helped Samsung's foundry division, whose losses reportedly shrank 41% from 6.74 trillion won in 2025 to 3.92 trillion won in 2026. Those figures are cited from an earlier estimate rather than final results.

The story rests on a single unnamed report and has not been confirmed by Nvidia, Samsung, Micron, SK hynix or TSMC. If accurate, it would strengthen TSMC's role as a manufacturing partner for memory and could increase demand for its 3nm capacity, while showing Nvidia's leverage over its memory suppliers.
stories.likelihood_reason: Specific details and a plausible supply-chain logic, but a single report with no named source and no company confirmation.

No confirmation from Nvidia, Samsung, Micron, SK hynix or TSMC
Specific technical figures suggest some insider input
stories.market_take: If confirmed, it would benefit TSMC's 3nm demand and Nvidia's supply position, with mixed implications for memory makers.

stories.story:
The Financial Times reports that Accenture, the world's largest IT consultancy, is looking to sell its operations in China. The potential deal is valued at up to $1.5bn. The available text is only a short feed summary, so the report's detail on buyers, timing and structure is not visible here.

The summary also says Accenture's shares have fluctuated in recent months over questions about how AI will affect its consulting and outsourcing business. Consultancies have been under scrutiny as clients explore whether AI can perform work once billed by the hour or by project. The article does not say whether the Chinese sale is linked to that pressure.

If the sale goes ahead, it would reduce Accenture's exposure to China, a market where foreign consultancies have faced growing competition and political sensitivity. It would also be a sign of portfolio pruning. Since the FT has reported the sale as a look, not a signed agreement, the outcome is uncertain. Accenture has not been quoted in this summary, and any final figure could differ from the reported maximum.
